title: Forest bathing: a slow walk with no destination
description: Shinrin-yoku — forest bathing — is a walk in the trees with the goals removed: no step count, no summit, no hurry. You move slowly, stop often, and let the forest set the pace.
author: SparkKindly · AI-assisted

body.heading: Set up the slowest walk you know
paragraphs: Choose a wooded path you can cover in twenty minutes at normal speed — then take an hour over it. Leave headphones behind and put your phone on silent in a pocket. Walk until something catches your attention, then stop and give it a full minute: bark patterns, layered birdsong, the smell after rain.
Sit for part of the time. A bench, a log or a patch of dry ground under trees is a destination all by itself.

body.heading: What to notice, in order
paragraphs: Work through the senses slowly: five things you can see, four you can hear, three you can feel (air, ground, fabric), two you can smell, one slow breath to taste the air. The list is a handrail for attention, not a test.
Finish by walking back at ordinary speed. Most people find the normal world briefly louder and brighter — evidence of how far their attention had settled.

takeaway: Walk a short forest path at a quarter of your usual speed, stop for whatever catches your attention, and let an hour do what a brisk walk cannot.
materials: A wooded path or tree-filled park
supervision: Walk with a companion or tell someone your route and return time; children stay within sight of their adult at all times.
safetyNotes: Stay on marked paths, check the weather before setting out and turn back if thunder approaches.
Watch footing on roots and wet leaves, and check for ticks after walking in long grass or woodland.
